summary: Defines an LDAP schema, object classes and attributes for printers and print services, based on the Printer attributes of RFC 2911. It lets directories store printer information.

eli5.summary: A phone-book layout for printers, so you can look up what each can do.

questions: what is the ldap printer schema
subtitle: A directory schema that lets LDAP describe printers: their names, locations, capabilities and how to reach them.

tldr.problem: Print clients need a vendor-neutral way to find printers and learn what they can do, and directories that speak LDAP had no shared definition of a Printer entry.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines six object classes and 41 attribute types. Most are drawn from the Internet Printing Protocol model (RFC 2911), Printer MIB v2 and PWG specifications, and they describe a printer's name, location, URIs, formats, media and features.
tldr.outcome: Directory entries for printers can be created or extended in a consistent way, including for the PWG IPP Everywhere project. RFC 7612 obsoletes RFC 3712 and adds seven new attribute types.

today: RFC 7612 is an Informational Independent Submission that obsoletes RFC 3712; the unit metadata lists nothing that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose and Sources
sections.content:
This document defines object classes and attribute types so that applications using the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP, RFC 4510) can describe Printers in a directory. It can be used for entries with common Printer information and to extend existing entries with Service Location Protocol (RFC 2608), Internet Printing Protocol/1.1 (RFC 2911) and lineprinter (RFC 1179) information.

The schema is based on the Printer attributes of RFC 2911 (Appendix E, taken from Section 4.4), plus selected attributes from Printer MIB v2 (RFC 3805), PWG 5107.2, PWG 5100.13 and PWG 5100.14, "IPP Everywhere". It is an Independent Submission by the IPP Working Group of the IEEE-ISTO Printer Working Group. It is also technically aligned with the IANA-registered SLP service:printer: v2.0 template, so simpler syntaxes are sometimes used.
sections.eli5: People who make printers and phone books agreed on one standard form for describing a printer, so any computer can read any printer's card.

sections.title: Design Choices for Strings and Matching
sections.content:
Almost all new attributes use the DirectoryString syntax, which is UTF-8. This covers URIs, descriptions in any language, and keywords. The keyword attributes can be extended with site-specific or vendor-specific names. The printer-natural-language-configured attribute holds a language tag for the description attributes.

Equality and substring matching use caseIgnoreMatch and caseIgnoreSubstringsMatch. For URIs this follows the spirit of the URI standard, which treats the host part case-insensitively; the RFC admits that either choice is a compromise. Case-insensitive matching is friendlier for descriptions and keywords and is mandatory for IEEE 1284 Device IDs. No new syntaxes or matching rules are defined.
sections.eli5: The card is written so that capital letters do not matter when you search, which makes it easier to find 'Room 123' even if someone typed 'room 123'.

sections.title: The Six Object Classes
sections.content:
The object classes are slpServicePrinter (auxiliary, for SLP-registered Printers), printerAbstract (abstract base for all Printer classes), printerService (structural), printerServiceAuxClass (auxiliary), printerIPP (auxiliary, for IPP Printers) and printerLPR (auxiliary, for LPR Printers; it requires printer-name).

printerAbstract lists the common attributes as optional, and both printerService and printerServiceAuxClass inherit them and add printer-uri and printer-xri-supported. The RFC's examples: use printerService for ordinary Printer entries, add slpServicePrinter for SLP-registered ones, add both printerLPR and printerIPP for printers that support both, and use printerServiceAuxClass to extend other structural classes. When extending other structural classes, printerService SHOULD NOT be used.
sections.eli5: There is a basic printer card, plus add-on stickers for printers that speak particular languages, so each printer carries only the stickers it needs.

sections.title: The Attribute Types
sections.content:
Section 4 defines 41 attribute types, each with an OID, matching rules and notes. Many are renamed IPP attributes, prefixed with printer- to avoid clashes in the flat LDAP namespace. Examples are printer-name, printer-location, printer-info, printer-make-and-model, printer-document-format-supported, printer-color-supported, printer-sides-supported and printer-media-supported. Others come from Printer MIB v2, such as printer-current-operator and printer-service-person.

printer-uri is single-valued, and if printer-xri-supported is used, that URI MUST be listed in it. Each printer-xri-supported value is a URI plus optional auth and sec fields, each ended by <, for example uri=ipp://example.com/ipp< auth=digest< sec=tls<. A missing auth or sec is read as none. Implementations SHOULD NOT exceed the underlying string length limits, such as 1023 octets for printer-uri and 255 for printer-name. Unknown optional values SHOULD NOT be set.
sections.eli5: Each line on the printer card has a name, like 'room' or 'can print in color', and rules for what can be written there and how long it can be.

sections.title: New Attributes and Changes from RFC 3712
sections.content:
Seven attribute types are new, registered by IANA from the base OID the IEEE-ISTO PWG received from IBM in October 2011: printer-device-id, printer-device-service-count, printer-uuid, printer-charge-info, printer-charge-info-uri, printer-geo-location and printer-ipp-features-supported. They hold an IEEE 1284 Device ID, a count of Printer instances (where -1 means unknown), a UUID URN, paid-printing details, a geo: URI such as geo:13.4125,103.8667, and the IPP features a Printer supports, such as ipp-everywhere.

Appendix A lists other changes from RFC 3712: editorial fixes, notes in place of length limits in the formal definitions, clearer treatment of the < and > field delimiters, and added notes on Unicode normalization and control characters. All object classes and the older attributes keep the OIDs that IBM assigned in March 2000 for RFC 3712.
sections.eli5: The new version adds a few new lines to the card, like a unique ID number and the printer's spot on a map, and cleans up the instructions.

sections.title: Security and Internationalization
sections.content:
The RFC points to RFC 4513 for LDAP authentication and for using TLS to protect connections. It stresses access control: only administrators should be able to change Printer entries, otherwise a client could be fooled into sending print jobs to a malicious host, exposing printed documents. DEL and C0 or C1 control characters in names such as printer-name can also cause vulnerabilities. IPP deployment issues are covered in Section 8 of RFC 2911.

On internationalization, all string attributes are UTF-8, and the language tag in printer-natural-language-configured applies to them. Values SHOULD be normalized as in RFC 5198 and SHOULD NOT contain control characters other than HT, CR and LF.
sections.eli5: Only the office manager should be allowed to edit the printer cards. If anyone could, a trickster could point the card to a fake printer and read your papers.
